role: Candidate discussed at Saqifah Banu Sa'idah
summary: Sa'd ibn Ubadah (RA) was the chief of the Khazraj tribe of Madinah and one of the most prominent of all the Ansar. He was renowned for his generosity, his participation in all the Prophet's campaigns, and his role at the Saqifah Banu Sa'idah after the Prophet's death. He died in Syria around 14 AH without having pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr, a matter discussed by classical scholars with care and nuance.
biography:
Sa'd ibn Ubadah ibn Dulaym al-Ansari al-Khazraji was born around 555 CE in Madinah, making him considerably older than most of the Sahaba. He was the sayyid (chief) of the Khazraj — the larger of the two Ansari tribes — and by the time of the Prophet's arrival in Madinah was already a man of great wealth, generosity, and standing. He is described in the sources as a tall, imposing man who excelled in archery, swimming, and writing — rare accomplishments in Arabia at the time.

Sa'd took the second pledge of Aqabah with the Prophet ﷺ before the Hijrah, pledging to protect him as the Ansar would protect their own families. He was among the twelve leaders (nuqaba') chosen at Aqabah to represent and organise the Ansar. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, Sa'd welcomed him with warm hospitality and was a regular presence at his side. Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra records that he maintained a large household where he fed hundreds of guests — poor and rich alike — daily throughout his life. The Prophet ﷺ acknowledged his exceptional generosity, and the Sahaba considered it among his defining qualities.

Sa'd fought at the Battle of Badr (2 AH), Uhud (3 AH), al-Khandaq (5 AH), and all subsequent major campaigns. He carried the standard of the Ansar in multiple expeditions. At the Conquest of Makkah (8 AH), Sa'd carried the standard of the Ansar as the army entered. He called out: 'Today is the day of slaughter (malhamah), today sanctities will be made lawful!' — a declaration the Prophet ﷺ considered inappropriate for a day of mercy and amnesty. The Prophet ﷺ took the standard from him and gave it to his son Qays, or by some accounts ordered it transferred to prevent any bloodshed beyond what was necessary. This account is recorded by Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari.

The most discussed chapter of Sa'd's biography involves the Saqifah Banu Sa'idah — the gathering that took place immediately after the Prophet's death in 11 AH (632 CE), in which the question of succession was resolved. The Ansar gathered in Saqifah Banu Sa'idah, Sa'd's tribal meeting place, and proposed that the leadership should come from the Ansar given their service and sacrifice. Sa'd was the Ansar's candidate. The Muhajirun, led by Abu Bakr and Umar, arrived and argued powerfully that leadership must rest with Quraysh. After deliberation — and in circumstances described in different ways by the sources — Abu Bakr was given the bay'ah. Sa'd ibn Ubadah did not give his personal pledge (bay'ah) to Abu Bakr, nor subsequently to Umar. He left Madinah and went to Syria.

Classical scholars have treated Sa'd's position with careful respect. Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and Ibn Hajar in al-Isabah do not consider his abstention evidence of sin or opposition to the caliphate, understanding it as a deeply personal grief at a decision he did not accept — while noting that he neither organised opposition nor incited others against Abu Bakr's government. He lived the remainder of his life in the Hawran region of Syria and died there around 14 AH (636 CE), during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab.

The circumstances of his death are unusual. The sources — including al-Tabari and Ibn Sa'd — record that he was found dead, with no one having witnessed the cause. A poetic verse attributed to jinn was reportedly heard, claiming his death. Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah recounts this account but treats it as one of the traditions (akhbar) rather than firmly authenticated hadith. However he died, Sa'd passed without pledging bay'ah — a fact classical scholars have never used to diminish his immense rank among the Ansar, his unquestioned early sacrifices, or his status as a companion of the Prophet ﷺ.

key_events.event: Took the second pledge of Aqabah; appointed one of the twelve leaders (nuqaba') of the Ansar
Fought at the Battle of Badr
Carried the Ansar standard at the Conquest of Makkah; the Prophet ﷺ redirected the standard over his words
Ansar's candidate at the Saqifah; did not give bay'ah to Abu Bakr; left Madinah for Syria
Died in the Hawran region of Syria

notable_traits: Legendary generosity — fed hundreds of guests daily throughout his life
Chief of the Khazraj and among the twelve naqibs chosen at Aqabah
Veteran of all major battles from Badr onwards
His abstention from bay'ah is treated by classical scholars as grief rather than rebellion

key_relationships.son: Qays ibn Sa'd ibn Ubadah — also a Companion and notable figure
key_relationships.parallel: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh — chief of the Aws (the other major Ansari tribe)
